Claessens et al. compressed 400 heterogeneous heat pump homes into one cluster-level DQN; after a month of simulation the agent reduced the electricity costs by 18% and shaves 0.9 MW (17%) off the evening peak [24]. Liu & Mao enrich the state of an actor–critic with one-hour PV and load forecast in a grid-tied single MG; the “information-enhanced” agent beats vanilla DDPG by 5.6 – 12.9% on cost while maintaining voltage inside ±5% [25]. Zhou et al. extended the idea to an electric-heat-gas microgrid where a continuous action DDPG co-optimizes battery and CHP, lowering daily costs by 6.8% with convergence in 300 episodes [26]. For networked microgrids, Tan et al. allowed each residential MG to train a Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) agent locally; the results of their approach reduced the average daily cost by 4.1% and training time by 38% [27]. Guo et al. approximated a Stackelberg equilibrium with a dual layer actor–critic; where the DSO was the price-setter, and the optimal dispatch was done by the MG agents. Equilibrium emerged within 250 episodes, boosting the DSO profit by 5% and reducing the MG costs by 4% [28]. Monfaredi et al. targeted an electric-thermal cluster in a grid-tied multi-energy MG by combining MADDPG with stacked denoising auto-encoders. When tested on an IEEE 33 bus and 8 node gas grid, costs fell by 9% and CO2 emissions fell by 8% [29]. Hedayatnia et al. decoupled training and execution, splitting an offline optimal EMS phase into an online DRL policy. Their results showed the MG cost dropped by 12.9% and run-time by 17% relative to a dueling-DQN baseline, while transmission losses reduced by 6% [30]. Gao et al. injected graph-attention and entropy annealing into Soft-Actor–Critic for a six MG cluster. The algorithm reduced operating costs by 10.2% and RES curtailment by 14.7% [31]. Wang et al. proposed a data-driven multi-agent stochastic-game RL for a networked microgrid with the goal of minimizing costs and improving grid stability [32]. Samadi et al. complemented these advances with a fully decentralized, multi-agent RL where self-interested DER and customer agents learn cost optimal bids via actor–critic algorithms, while an upper-level manager clears local electricity-and-heat trades without exposing raw data. Their results during testing finalized transactions in <2 s, increased the aggregator’s revenue by 5%, and reduced total MG costs by 7% [33]. Yang et al. deployed a Rainbow deep-RL controller that jointly scheduled a wind-farm battery and reserve purchases. By directly mapping forecasted wind and price trajectories to continuous charge/discharge actions, the agent absorbed forecast error automatically and increased the utility’s revenue in every simulated market scenario [34]. Foruzan et al. demonstrated that even a tabular multi-agent RL scheme where each generator, storage unit and customer learns autonomously can drive an islanded MG toward a Nash equilibrium dispatch that lowers fuel use and unmet load probability [35]. Vergara et al. extended RL to inverter-level services where a decentralized actor–critic scheme dispatches on each PV inverter every few seconds and converges to near optimal voltage regulation, limiting additional PV curtailment to <2.5% [36]. Zhou et al. combined deeplearning forecasts with a lightweight DDPG agent for battery scheduling in an integrated energy MG; the RL policy cuts solution time by 61% while sacrificing only 3.1% reductions in cost accuracy relative to an MILP, a trade-off that is crucial for real-time operation [26]. Going beyond electricity-only systems, Zhang et al. framed carbon-capture and power-to-gas dispatch as a Markov game and trained a prioritized experience replay Soft-Actor–Critic (SAC). They observed that when prediction errors exceeded 10%, their PER-SAC reduced total cost by approximately 11.6% [37].
